stem: A market research firm wants to study the buying habits of shoppers in a large city. The city is divided into 80 wards, and a random sample of 8 wards is selected. Data is then collected from every household in each of the selected 8 wards. This sampling method is best described as:

options.text: Stratified sampling, because the city is divided into groups
Systematic sampling, because a fixed number of wards is selected
Cluster sampling, because entire groups (wards) are selected and then all units within them are surveyed
Simple random sampling, because wards are chosen randomly

per_option_rationale.rationale: Stratified sampling requires drawing a random sub-sample from each and every stratum; here only 8 out of 80 wards are selected and the remaining 72 are not sampled at all, which is the defining feature of cluster sampling.
Systematic sampling selects individual units at a fixed interval from an ordered list; selecting entire wards is not interval-based selection of individual units.
Cluster sampling: the population is divided into clusters (wards), a random sample of clusters is selected, and all units within the chosen clusters are observed. Both defining features are present.

Simple random sampling selects individual units (not whole groups) such that every individual has an equal chance of selection; selecting clusters (wards) and surveying all their members is not simple random sampling.

explanation: The two-stage structure identifies cluster sampling: (1) the population is partitioned into naturally-occurring groups (clusters = wards), (2) a random sample of clusters is chosen, and (3) all elements in the selected clusters are observed.

explanation_sections.punchline: The decisive feature is that entire naturally-occurring groups (wards) are selected and every member within them is surveyed - that is cluster sampling, not stratified (which samples from every stratum).
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: cluster sampling. Define the clusters (wards), confirm that only selected clusters are sampled and all units within them are observed. Contrast with stratified: in stratified sampling, every group is sampled; in cluster sampling, only randomly selected groups are sampled.
explanation_sections.lesson: Cluster vs. stratified: in cluster sampling, not all clusters are sampled (cost efficiency); in stratified sampling, every stratum is sampled (representational accuracy).
explanation_sections.timing: 40 seconds. The key distinction: if every group is sampled - stratified; if only some groups are sampled (all members surveyed within selected groups) - cluster.
